question: A disease will kill 600 people unless you act. Which programme do you choose?
answer: Most people take the sure thing when it is worded as lives saved, and the gamble when it is worded as deaths. In Tversky and Kahneman's study, 72% chose to save 200 for sure; only 22% chose the same plan worded as 400 dying. Every option leaves 200 alive on average. Only the words moved.
move: Before choosing, say the option the other way round: saved as died, gain as loss.

questions.prompt: Now the same 600, with programme C or D:

scene.why: A sure gain feels safe; a sure loss feels unbearable, so we gamble to dodge it.
scene.same: You held steady. The crowd didn't: the sure plan fell from 72% to 22%.
scene.switched: You switched, like most people. A and C are the same plan; so are B and D.

reference: Tversky & Kahneman, The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice, Science 211 (1981): 453-458

question: Free money, from a 1995 Dutch study in guilders. Which offer would you take?
answer: Waiting four weeks for 10% more feels costly when the wait starts today, and cheap when it starts in six months. In Keren and Roelofsma's study, 82% took 100 now over 110 in four weeks; only 37% took 100 in 26 weeks over 110 in 30. Same trade, minus the word now.
move: Push both dates a year away and check you still choose the same.

scene.why: Now gets a bonus in the mind that no later date gets, so a wait from today feels longer.
scene.same: You held steady. The crowd didn't: taking the 100 fell from 82% to 37%.
scene.switched: You switched, like many in the study. Both times it was 4 weeks for 10 more.

source: Keren & Roelofsma, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1995
reference: Keren & Roelofsma, Immediacy and certainty in intertemporal choice, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 63 (1995): 287-297

question: Picture a room of drivers your age. Are you a more skilful driver than half of them?
answer: Only half of a room can be better than half of it. Yet when Ola Svenson asked American students to rank their driving skill against the others in the room, 93% put themselves in the top half; Swedish students, 69%. We see our own care from the inside, and others only through their mistakes.
move: Before ranking yourself, ask how the people below you would rank you.

options.label: Better than half
options.mirror: So did 93% of the students asked. At most half a room can sit in its top half.

options.label: Not better than half
options.mirror: Only 7% said this. Humble or right, you saw what the rest of the room missed.

scene.why: We judge ourselves by our intentions and careful moments, and others by the slips we see.

reference: Svenson, Are we all less risky and more skillful than our fellow drivers?, Acta Psychologica 47 (1981): 143-148
